core: Working definition: brain structures are the named regions of the brain that carry out different jobs (attributed to OpenStax Psychology 2e: the brain divides into forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain)
The forebrain: cerebral cortex, frontal lobe, parietal lobe, temporal lobe, occipital lobe, limbic system — one line each on general role, with original examples
The midbrain and hindbrain: brainstem (basic life support) and cerebellum (balance, coordination, movement) — one line each
The two hemispheres: left and right work together via the corpus callosum; the honest note that the 'left brain/right brain' myth oversimplifies the evidence
Localization: some functions lean on specific regions (Broca's area, primary visual cortex), but the brain works as a connected system
How we know: brain damage (strokes, Phineas Gage, Broca's-area cases) and brain imaging (CT, MRI, fMRI, PET, EEG), each named with one line
Honest framing: the brain is a city of neighborhoods, not a machine of separate parts
supporting: Contralateral control: the left hemisphere controls the right side of the body and vice versa
The corpus callosum (~200 million axons) as the main connection between hemispheres
Lateralization research is real but inconsistent; the interactive view is the accurate one
Broca's area (speech production) and Wernicke's area (speech comprehension) as classic localization examples

claims.claim: The brain and its parts can be divided into three main categories: the forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain.
The forebrain is the largest part of the brain; it contains the cerebral cortex and subcortical structures such as the limbic system.

The cerebral cortex is the layer of gray matter that covers the outside of the cerebral hemispheres and is associated with higher cognitive functions, such as language, learning, perception, and planning.
Each cerebral hemisphere is subdivided into four lobes — frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital — each associated with different functions.
The frontal lobe is involved in reasoning, motor control, emotion, and language, and contains the motor cortex, the prefrontal cortex, and Broca's area, which is essential for language production.
The parietal lobe processes sensory information from across the body, such as touch, temperature, and pain, via the somatosensory cortex.
The temporal lobe is associated with hearing, memory, emotion, and some aspects of language, and contains the auditory cortex and Wernicke's area, which is important for speech comprehension.
The occipital lobe is located at the very back of the brain and contains the primary visual cortex, which is responsible for interpreting incoming visual information.
The limbic system is a collection of structures beneath the cortex, including the hippocampus, amygdala, and hypothalamus, that is involved in processing emotion and memory.
The brainstem connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord, includes the midbrain, pons, and medulla, and is involved in basic life-support functions such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure.
The cerebellum is a structure at the back of the brain that coordinates balance, movement, and motor skills, and is also associated with procedural memory.

The brain is a bilateral structure: the left hemisphere controls the right half of the body and the right hemisphere controls the left half; the two hemispheres are connected by the corpus callosum, a thick band of about 200 million axons that lets each side share information.

There is evidence of specialization of function (lateralization) in each hemisphere, mainly regarding language, but research on which hemisphere dominates various behaviors has produced inconsistent results, and it is better to think of how the two hemispheres interact to produce a behavior than to attribute behaviors to one hemisphere; the popular 'left brain/right brain' dichotomy oversimplifies.

Localization of function is the concept that specific parts of the cerebral cortex are relatively specialized for particular types of cognitive and behavioral processes, yet all of the areas of the brain interact with one another to provide the foundation for thoughts and behaviors.

Much of what psychologists know about the functions of different brain areas comes from studying changes in the behavior and ability of individuals who have suffered damage to the brain, such as stroke patients and the historical case of Phineas Gage.

Brain imaging techniques let researchers see the structure and activity of the living brain: CT uses x-rays to construct structural images, MRI uses magnetic fields to show structure in detail, fMRI tracks blood flow and oxygen levels to show activity over time, PET uses a radioactive tracer to map active areas, and EEG records the brain's electrical activity with millisecond accuracy.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The popular 'left brain/right brain' idea says people are either logical (left) or creative (right), while the research on lateralization paints a messier picture.
positions: There is genuine evidence of specialization, especially for language, which leans left for most people (OpenStax 3.4 lateralization section).
Research on which hemisphere dominates various behaviors has produced inconsistent results (OpenStax 3.4, citing Banich & Heller).
Researchers recommend thinking about how the two hemispheres interact to produce a given behavior rather than attributing behaviors to one hemisphere (OpenStax 3.4).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches that hemispheric specialization is real but limited, that both hemispheres are involved in nearly every behavior, and that the pop-culture personality dichotomy oversimplifies the evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Localization of function versus a systems view: is each function owned by one brain region?
positions: Specific areas are relatively specialized for particular processes, e.g., the occipital lobe for vision and Broca's area for language production (APA Dictionary 'localization of function'; OpenStax 3.4).
All of the areas of the brain interact with one another to provide the foundation for thoughts and behaviors (OpenStax 3.4 introduction).
After damage, other regions can partly take over, as seen in recovery and imaging studies (OpenStax 3.4 stroke and recovery discussion).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents localization as a real tendency within an interactive system: functions lean on regions, but the brain works as a connected whole.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Imaging language: do fMRI 'hot spots' prove a region is the cause of a behavior?
positions: fMRI tracks blood flow and oxygen levels as indirect markers of activity, with limited temporal precision (OpenStax 3.4).
EEG records electrical activity with millisecond accuracy but gives less spatial detail (OpenStax 3.4).
PET requires a radioactive tracer and shows little detail, which is why fMRI largely replaced it (OpenStax 3.4).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes each technique's actual method and limits, and presents imaging as one evidence stream that converges with brain-damage studies rather than a direct photograph of thought.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft described the topic as 'a foundational concept in Psychology' and 'a concept students use to organize information' with no factual content; no such claims were carried forward.
The draft's vocabulary entry 'Brain Structures: A foundational Psychology concept covered in this lesson' was circular and was replaced with source-verified definitions.
The draft's Eli-10 compared brain structures to 'a label on a toolbox drawer'; the metaphor was replaced with the verified city-of-neighborhoods framing tied to actual structures.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft boilerplate with source-verified content: the three-division map (forebrain/midbrain/hindbrain), each forebrain structure's role, brainstem and cerebellum roles, hemisphere integration, and the localization nuance.
Added the honest note on the left-brain/right-brain myth, grounded in OpenStax's statement that hemispheric-dominance research is inconsistent and the interactive view is preferred.
Added the honest localization note (functions lean on regions, but all areas interact) and the city-not-machine framing.

Built entirely original examples (planning a study schedule, pebble in the shoe, friend's voice on the phone, catching a ball, song-evoked memory, pianist's fingers, fictional stroke patient Marta) instead of reproducing source vignettes.
Named each imaging technique (CT, MRI, fMRI, PET, EEG) with one line on how it works, per the source material.
